paragraphs.title: The Leaders Are Accused of Exploiting the People

answers: The heads of Jacob and the princes of the house of Israel
The prophets only
All the nations of the world
easy.explanation: Micah addresses the heads of Jacob and the princes of the house of Israel.
easy.q: To whom does Micah speak at the beginning of the passage?

answers: They hate judgment and love peace
They hate the good and love the evil
They hate riches and love poverty
easy.explanation: The passage says that they hate the good and love the evil.
easy.q: What do the leaders hate, and what do they love?

answers: The LORD will answer them immediately
The LORD will send them riches
The LORD will not hear them and will hide His face
easy.explanation: Because of their evil deeds, the LORD will not hear them.
easy.q: What will happen when the leaders cry unto the LORD?

answers: Their position requires them to act justly
So they can learn how to collect taxes
So they can choose new prophets
medium.explanation: Their responsibility was to know and practice judgment, but they had failed.
medium.q: Why does Micah remind the leaders that they should know judgment?

answers: Right and fair decisions
A royal feast
A military victory
medium.explanation: “Judgment” refers to justice and the fair treatment of others.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does the word “judgment” mean in this passage?

answers: Their wrongdoing brings judgment upon them
Their wrongdoing causes the people to stop crying
The passage shows no connection
medium.explanation: The LORD’s refusal to hear them is presented as a consequence of their evil conduct.
medium.q: What is the connection between the leaders’ evil deeds and the LORD’s refusal to answer?

answers: The contrast between riches and poverty only
The leaders’ duty to practice judgment and their oppression of the people
The contrast between Jerusalem and Zion
challenge.explanation: The leaders should know judgment, yet they hate good and mistreat the people.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the passage?

answers: The cruelty and severity of the leaders’ exploitation
The importance of feast days
The work of the priests in the temple
challenge.explanation: The graphic comparison portrays the leaders as violently consuming and abusing the people.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with meat in a pot and flesh in a caldron emphasize?

answers: They seek God in trouble but do not change their ways
They always act according to judgment
They do not know that the LORD exists
challenge.explanation: Their cry comes after their wrongdoing and does not show genuine repentance.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the leaders cry to the LORD only after harming the people?

paragraphs.title: Condemnation of Prophets Dependent on Support

answers: To the people who support them
To those who rebuke them
To those who refuse to hear them
easy.explanation: They announce peace to those who put food into their mouths.
easy.q: To whom do the misleading prophets cry, “Peace”?

answers: They bless him
They prepare war against him
They always ignore him
easy.explanation: The KJV says that they prepare war against the person who does not provide for them.
easy.q: What do the prophets do to the person who does not support them?

answers: Riches and honor
Power by the spirit of the LORD, judgment, and might
Food and clothing
easy.explanation: Micah says he is full of power by the spirit of the LORD, judgment, and might.
easy.q: What does Micah say that he is full of?

answers: They lead or mislead the people into error
They protect the people from danger
They teach the people wisdom
medium.explanation: The phrase means that the prophets lead the people in a wrong direction.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does it mean that the prophets “make my people err”?

answers: The person’s wisdom
Whether the person supports them and puts food into their mouths
The person’s place of residence
medium.explanation: Their message changes according to whether they receive support.
medium.q: What causes the prophets to say “Peace” to one person and prepare war against another?

answers: He is filled with the spirit of the LORD, judgment, and might
He receives money from the leaders
He promises peace to everyone
medium.explanation: Micah connects his ability to rebuke sin with divine power, judgment, and courage.
medium.q: Why is Micah able to declare Jacob’s transgression and Israel’s sin?

answers: The misleading prophets depend on support, while Micah emphasizes God’s spirit, judgment, and courage
The misleading prophets are silent, while Micah does not speak
The misleading prophets practice judgment, while Micah seeks money
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts paid messages with Micah’s Spirit-empowered declaration of truth.
challenge.q: What is the contrast between the misleading prophets and Micah?

answers: Great success in their prophecy
The loss of vision and divine revelation
The beginning of the rainy season
challenge.explanation: Night, darkness, and the lack of an answer represent the withdrawal of prophetic revelation.
challenge.q: What does the darkness coming upon the prophets symbolize?

answers: It shows that they no longer have an answer from God
They have lost their money
They refuse to speak with the people
challenge.explanation: They are ashamed because there is no answer of God.
challenge.q: Why is the shame of the seers and diviners significant?

paragraphs.title: Corruption of the Leadership and Public Institutions

answers: Judgment
Riches
Prophecy
easy.explanation: The leaders are described as those who abhor judgment.
easy.q: What do the leaders abhor according to the passage?

answers: With wisdom and peace
With blood and iniquity
With work and righteousness
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity.”
easy.q: How are Zion and Jerusalem built?

answers: Reward, hire, and money
Prayer, fasting, and mercy
War, trade, and farming
easy.explanation: The heads judge for reward, the priests teach for hire, and the prophets divine for money.
easy.q: What motivates the heads, priests, and prophets?

answers: To twist or corrupt every fair judgment
To preserve and defend justice
To make every decision straight and fair
medium.explanation: The phrase means that the leaders corrupt what is right and fair.
medium.q: What does “pervert all equity” mean in this passage?

answers: All the officials act in exchange for payment
The leaders refuse every public office
The priests and prophets refuse to speak
medium.explanation: The heads, priests, and prophets each serve for reward, hire, or money.
medium.q: How is corruption shown throughout the public system?

answers: That the LORD does not exist
That the LORD is among them, so no evil can come upon them
That the LORD punishes only prophets
medium.explanation: They trust that the LORD is among them and therefore assume that no evil will come upon them.
medium.q: What false claim do the leaders make about the LORD?

answers: Corruption allows the cities to be built through blood and iniquity
Straight judgment causes the cities to be destroyed
The passage connects judgment and construction in no way
challenge.explanation: The corruption of the leaders is linked with buildings established through violence and wrongdoing.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between corrupt judgment and the building of Zion and Jerusalem?

answers: Corruption affects several institutions and classes of leaders
Only the prophets are guilty
The priests have no connection with leadership
challenge.explanation: The passage presents corruption among political, religious, and prophetic officials.
challenge.q: What does the sequence of heads, priests, and prophets emphasize?

answers: They use religious confidence as an excuse while practicing injustice
They do not know where Jerusalem is
They obey every requirement of judgment
challenge.explanation: They expect divine protection while continuing to corrupt justice and oppress others.
challenge.q: Why is their confidence in the LORD shown to be false?

paragraphs.title: The Foretold Destruction of Zion and Jerusalem

answers: A field that is plowed
A fortified city
A palace
easy.explanation: The verse says that Zion shall be plowed as a field.

answers: A flourishing garden
Heaps of ruins
A center of trade
easy.explanation: Jerusalem shall become heaps, meaning ruined heaps or piles of destruction.

answers: The high places of the forest
A marketplace
A spring
easy.explanation: The mountain of the house will become like the high places of the forest.
easy.q: What will the mountain of the house become?

answers: Piles or mounds of ruins
New houses
Fertile fields
medium.explanation: “Heaps” describes the piles of rubble left after destruction.
medium.q: In the KJV, what are “heaps” in the description of Jerusalem?

answers: The sins and injustice of the leaders
A lack of water alone
The people’s desire to build a new city
medium.explanation: The destruction comes “for your sake,” referring to the leaders’ guilt and wrongdoing.
medium.q: What is the stated reason for the destruction described in the verse?

answers: Zion becomes a field, Jerusalem becomes heaps, and the mountain of the house becomes wooded high places
Jerusalem becomes a field, Zion becomes a forest, and the mountain becomes a palace
The mountain becomes a field, Zion becomes a palace, and Jerusalem becomes a forest
medium.explanation: This is the exact order given in Micah 3:12.
medium.q: What order of changes does the verse describe?

answers: The leaders’ injustice will bring the loss of the urban center
The cities will become politically stronger
The temple mount will expand into a greater city
challenge.explanation: Places of human settlement and government will be reduced to a field, ruins, and wooded high places.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between the former cities and their future condition teach?

answers: It presents the expected result of the leaders’ injustice and corruption
It cancels Micah’s criticism of the leaders
It promises that the leaders will escape
challenge.explanation: The destruction is the judgment associated with the sins condemned throughout the chapter.
challenge.q: How does the final verse relate to the warnings in the earlier verses?

answers: The place will lose its settled and built character
The place will become a larger government center
The place will remain unchanged
challenge.explanation: The images describe desolation and the removal of the former built-up settlement.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the change from an inhabited city to a field, ruins, and forest?
